title: Big change coming on October 1, banks panic
full_text:
Australia’s biggest banks are hiking credit card fees and slashing rewards perks for customers as they try to claw back millions in revenue ahead of the Reserve Bank of Australia’s surcharge ban.
From October 1, surcharging on debit and credit cards will be banned and caps on interchange fees will be lowered. Interchange fees are paid by businesses to banks each time a card transaction is processed, with the fees used by banks to fund rewards programs.
The RBA estimates this could cost banks about $660 million annually, and banks are now moving to recoup this through dramatic changes to their rewards credit cards.
Millions of Aussies are expected to flock to ATMs all over the country to withdraw cash on Tuesday as part of a major campaign.
MORE: ‘Hard’: Horror spike gives RBA no choice
Canstar director of data insights Sally Tindall told news.com.au major banks including Commonwealth Bank, Westpac and its subsidiaries St.George, Bank of Melbourne and BankSA, and NAB had all announced changes to their offerings.
“What we’ve seen is a really broad range of different ways to cut value from those rewards cards, which includes hikes to card fees and hikes to interest rates,” Ms Tindall said.
CBA is overhauling its rewards credit cards to bring them under its expanded CommBank Yello loyalty scheme. From September 29, the earn rate for cardholders will be based on their Yello tier or how many products you have with the bank.
It’s also scrapping card fee waivers and replacing them with vouchers, and cutting some insurance coverage.
Westpac and its subsidiaries are hiking interest rates on rewards cards by up to 3 per cent and upping annual fees. The Qantas Platinum card, for example, will see its annual fee increase from $75 to $125.
St.George, Bank of Melbourne and Bank SA are also cutting interest-free periods down from up to 55 days, to up to 45 days.
“Across both Westpac and CBA, we’ve seen a hike to the burn rate. So basically people will have to earn more points in order to redeem a reward and that can really sting,” Ms Tindall said.
NAB is hiking its interest rates by 1.5 per cent and changing earn rates from October 1. On its NAB Qantas Rewards Premium card, for example, customers will go from earning 1 point per $1.50 for the first $3,000 spent, to 1 point per $2 spent.
ANZ is yet to announce ongoing rewards changes, but it has cut the sign-up points available on its popular Frequent Flyer Black and Platinum credit cards.
It slashed the bonus on its Black card from 130,000 to 80,000 Qantas points, and scrapped a $200 cashback offer for new customers. The bonus on its Platinum card was cut from 75,000 to 40,000, with the $100 credit for new customers axed.
Point Hacks spokesperson Daniel Sciberras told news.com.au banks were pulling various levers “across the board” in response to the interchange fee change.
“I think of one bank that’s pulled the lever more on reducing the welcome bonus, there’s others that have pulled the levers on the earn rate or the interest free period or introducing additional fees,” Mr Sciberras said.
“We’re not seeing a uniform reaction from the banks.”
RBA surcharge ban a ‘circuit breaker’ for banks
The surcharge ban is expected to save Aussie consumers about $1.6 billion in surcharge fees each year, while businesses are set to save about $910 million per year.
The ban applies to EFTPOS, Mastercard and Visa. While American Express isn’t subject to the RBA’s surcharge ban, it is voluntarily changing its merchant rules so businesses will no longer be able to surcharge Amex cards from October 1.
The RBA will reduce the cap on interchange fees for credit cards from 0.8 to 0.3 per cent of the value of the transactions.
Ms Tindall said the upcoming cap on interchange fees would see charges reduced by up to 63 per cent for credit cards and it was clear banks weren’t willing to absorb the loss.
“The banks are using this as a circuit breaker to relook at exactly what’s offered in their rewards programs,” she said.
“People with rewards cards should do exactly the same. Use this as an opportunity to do a stock take of exactly whether you’re ahead or in the red from your card.
“And it could be potentially the circuit breaker that you need to get rid of the credit card altogether and move to paying with debit.”
A Money.com.au survey conducted in January found 18 per cent of Aussies would cancel their credit card if rewards were cut, while 33 per cent would switch to a lower-fee card.
Cardholders are being urged to get across the fine print of any changes, including changes to earn and burn rates.
Westpac, for example, currently requires 23,500 points to redeem a $100 eGift card. This will increase by 25 per cent to 29,412 come September 30.
In CBA’s current program, a $50 Myer card currently requires 10,950 points. But when it transfers over to the Yello program, it will increase to 12,500 points despite it being a “one-for-one” points transfer.
“So a lot of people that have racked up thousands of Awards points will see the value of those points drop overnight, at least in regards to that Myer gift card,” Ms Tindall said.
Ms Tindall recommended cardholders write down how much they have paid in fees over the last year and how much interest they have been charged.
Then compare this with the value of points redeemed, rather than collected, over the last 12 months and see if things stack up.
It could also be worth considering redeeming your points if they are set to go down in value.
